front: Define the term **magnet**.
back: A **magnet** is an object with a **north pole** and a **south pole**. It attracts magnetic materials and can attract or repel other magnets.

front: Define the term **magnetic material**.
back: A **magnetic material** is a material that is **attracted** to a magnet. It is attracted to **both poles** and can be **magnetised**.

front: Define the term **non-magnetic material**.
back: A **non-magnetic material** is **neither attracted nor repelled** by a magnet.

front: Which metals are **magnetic**?
back: The magnetic metals are **iron**, **cobalt** and **nickel**. **Steel** is also magnetic because it is an alloy containing iron.

front:
**True or False?**

Aluminium is a magnetic material.
back:
**False.**

**Aluminium** is not a magnetic material, so it is not attracted to a magnet.

front:
**True or False?**

Opposite poles attract.
back:
**True.**

A **north** pole and a **south** pole are opposite poles, so they **attract** each other.

front: Define the term **like poles**.
back: **Like poles** are poles of the same type, e.g. two north poles. Like poles **repel** each other.

front: How can you test whether an object is a **magnet**?
back:
Bring the object close to a known magnet:

- It is a **magnet** if it is **repelled** by the known magnet
- It is a **magnetic material** if it is only ever **attracted**
- It is a **non-magnetic material** if it is neither attracted nor repelled

front: What is **induced magnetism**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Induced magnetism** is when a magnetic material **temporarily becomes a magnet** while it is inside a magnetic **field**.

front: What happens to the ends of a magnetic material when magnetism is **induced** in it?
back: One end becomes a **north pole** and the other a **south pole**. The end **closest** to the magnet has the **opposite pole** to the magnet's nearest pole.

front:
**True or False?**

Induced magnets keep their magnetism after being removed from the magnetic field.
back:
**False.**

An induced magnet **loses its magnetism quickly** when it is removed from the magnetic field.

front:
**True or False?**

Induced magnetism can cause a magnet to repel a magnetic material. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

Induced magnetism **always** causes a force of **attraction** between the magnet and the induced magnet.

front: Define the term **permanent magnet**.
back: A **permanent magnet** produces its **own magnetic field** and does not lose its magnetism easily. Permanent magnets are made from materials such as **steel**.

front: Why is **steel** used for permanent magnets but **soft iron** used in electromagnets?
back: **Steel** stays magnetised for a long time, so it is used for **permanent magnets**. **Soft iron** loses its magnetism as soon as the cause of the induced magnetism is removed, so it is used in **electromagnets** and transformers.

front: An **electromagnet** is made by winding coils of wire around a **______** core.
back: An **electromagnet** is made by winding coils of wire around a **soft iron** core.

front:
**True or False?**

An electromagnet can be switched on and off.
back:
**True.**

The electromagnet is switched **on** when **current** flows through the coils and switched **off** when no current flows.

front: State three ways to increase the strength of an **electromagnet**.
back:
The strength of an electromagnet can be increased by:

- Increasing the **current**
- Increasing the **number of turns** of the coil
- Adding a **soft iron core**

front:
**True or False?**

The strength of a permanent magnet can be changed.
back:
**False.**

It is not possible to change the strength of a **permanent magnet**. Only an **electromagnet's** strength can be changed.

front: Give two uses of **permanent magnets**.
back:
Uses of permanent magnets include:

- Compasses
- Fridge magnets
- Toys
- School lab experiments

front: Give two uses of **electromagnets**.
back:
Uses of electromagnets include:

- MRI scanners
- Speakers and earphones
- Recycling (sorting scrap metal)
- Maglev trains

front: Define the term **magnetic field**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: A **magnetic field** is a region in which a **magnetic pole** experiences a **force**.

front: How is the direction of a magnetic field at a point defined? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The direction of a magnetic field at a point is the direction of the **force** on the **north pole** of a magnet at that point.

front: What are magnetic **field lines**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Field lines** are lines drawn around a magnet to represent its magnetic field. Each line has an **arrow** showing the **direction** of the field.

front: In which direction do magnetic field lines go? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Magnetic field lines always go **from** a **north** pole **to** a **south** pole.

front:
**True or False?**

The magnetic field is strongest at the poles of a bar magnet. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**True.**

The magnetic field is **strongest at the poles**, where the field lines are **closest together**.

front: How is the weakening of a bar magnet's field with distance shown by its field lines? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The magnetic field becomes **weaker** as the distance from the magnet increases, so the field lines get **further apart**.

front: How many **types** of electric charge are there?
back: There are **two** types of electric charge: **positive** and **negative**.

front: What are the **charges** of the particles inside an atom?
back:
- **Electrons** are negatively charged
- **Protons** are positively charged
- **Neutrons** are neutral (no charge)

front: Why is the overall charge of an atom **zero**?
back: An atom contains **equal numbers** of **protons** and **electrons**, so their equal and opposite charges **cancel out**.

front:
**True or False?**

Opposite charges attract.
back:
**True.**

Opposite charges **attract** each other.

front: What happens when two **like charges** are brought close together?
back: When two like charges are brought close together, they **repel** each other.

front: What **units** is electric charge measured in? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Electric charge is measured in **coulombs (C)**.

front: What is the purpose of rubbing **insulating solids** with a cloth in electrostatic experiments?
back: Rubbing transfers **electrons** between the cloth and the insulator, leaving them with **opposite** net charges.

front: When charging by friction, why does one insulator become **positively charged**?
back: Only **electrons** can move. The insulator that **loses electrons** is left with a net **positive charge**, while the insulator that **gains electrons** becomes **negatively charged**.

front: Why does charge **remain** on an insulator after it has been charged by friction?
back: The charges **cannot immediately flow away**, because insulators do not conduct.

front: Give **two** simple methods of showing that an object is electrically charged.
back:
Any two from:

- using it to pick up small pieces of paper
- sticking a charged balloon to a wall by attraction
- using it to pull a stream of water towards it
- bringing it close to another charged rod

front: Describe an experiment to demonstrate electrostatic charging by friction.
back:
- **Suspend** an insulating rod in a cradle using a length of thread so it can rotate freely
- **Rub** one end of the rod with a cloth to give it a charge
- Charge one end of a second insulating rod by rubbing it with a cloth
- Hold the charged end of the second rod close to the charged end of the first rod and observe whether it **attracts** or **repels**

front: How can you determine whether two charged rods have the **same charge**?
back:
Observe their interaction when brought close together.

- If they **repel** each other, they have the **same** charge
- If they **attract** each other, they have **opposite** charges

front: Why can a **negatively charged** comb pick up small, uncharged pieces of paper?
back: The **positive charges** in the paper are attracted to the surface closest to the comb. Opposite charges attract, so the paper sticks to the comb due to **electrostatic attraction**.

front: Define **electric field**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: An **electric field** is a region of space in which an electric charge experiences a **force**.

front: How is the **direction** of an electric field at a point defined? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The direction of an electric field at a point is the direction of the **force** on a **positive charge** at that point.

front:
**True or False?**

Electric fields always point towards positive charges. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

The direction of an electric field is the direction of the force on a **positive charge**, so electric fields point **away from** positive charges and **towards** negative charges.

front: What creates an **electric field**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Charged objects** create electric fields around themselves, similar to how magnets create magnetic fields.

front: Why is an electric field a **vector** quantity? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: An electric field has both **magnitude** (strength) and **direction**.

front: Define **conductor**.
back: A **conductor** is a material that allows **charge** (usually electrons) to flow through it easily.

front:
**True or False?**

Metals are generally good insulators.
back:
**False.**

The best conductors tend to be **metals**.

front: Why do metals conduct electricity very well?
back:
- Metals are made up of positively charged metal ions with their outermost electrons **delocalised**, meaning the electrons are **free to move**
- Current is the rate of flow of electrons, so the more easily electrons are able to flow, the **better** the conductor

front: Define **insulator**.
back: An **insulator** is a material that has **no free charges**, so it does **not** allow charge to flow through it very easily.

front:
**True or False?**

Insulators allow no charge at all to pass through them.
back:
**False.**

Some non-metals, such as **wood**, allow **some** charge to pass through them. Insulators can conduct a little in the form of **static** electricity.

front: Give **two** examples of electrical conductors and **two** examples of electrical insulators.
back:
Conductors — any two from:

- silver
- copper
- aluminium
- steel

Insulators — any two from:

- rubber
- plastic
- glass
- wood

front: Define **current**.
back: **Current** is the rate of flow of **electric charge**.

front: What is the purpose of an **ammeter**?
back: The purpose of an **ammeter** is to measure the **current** in a circuit.

front:
**True or False?**

Ammeters should be connected in parallel to measure current.
back:
**False.**

Ammeters should be connected in **series** with the component being measured.

front: Which is more accurate, a digital or an analogue ammeter?
back: A **digital ammeter** is more accurate than an analogue ammeter because it gives a specific value, is capable of displaying more precise values and can measure very small currents.

front: In metal wires, the current is a flow of negatively charged **______**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: In metal wires, the current is a flow of negatively charged **electrons**.

front: What is the equation relating current, charge and time? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The equation relating current, charge and time is:

$I = \frac{Q}{t}$

Where:

- $I$ = current, measured in amps (A)
- $Q$ = charge, measured in coulombs (C)
- $t$ = time, measured in seconds (s)

front: Define **conventional current**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Conventional current** is the flow of **positive** charge, from the **positive** terminal to the **negative** terminal of a cell.

front: How is electron flow different to conventional current? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Electrons** flow from the **negative** terminal to the **positive** terminal of a cell. This is the **opposite direction** to conventional current.

front: Define **direct current (d.c.)**.
back: **Direct current (d.c.)** is a steady current, constantly flowing in the same direction in a circuit, from positive to negative.

front: Define **alternating current (a.c.)**.
back: **Alternating current (a.c.)** is a current that continuously changes its direction, going back and forth around a circuit.

front: Sketch the graphs for d.c. and a.c.
back:
The graphs for d.c. and a.c. are

![Graphs of Direct Current (D.C.) and Alternating Current (A.C.). The D.C. graph shows a constant current over time, while the A.C. graph shows a sinusoidal wave varying over time.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-Flashcards/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-physics/electricity-and-magnetism/electrical-quantities/assets/70102f6603de-9345-ac-and-dc.png)

front:
**True or False?**

Cells and batteries are sources of d.c.
back:
**True.**

Cells and batteries produce **direct current (d.c.)**, while electrical generators, such as mains electricity, produce **alternating current (a.c.)**.

front:
**True or False?**

An a.c. power source involves a positive and negative terminal.
back:
**False.**

An a.c. power source involves **two identical terminals** that change from positive to negative and back again.

front: Name **three** sources that supply a voltage to a circuit.
back:
Three sources that supply a voltage to a circuit are:

- a **cell**
- a **battery** (multiple cells)
- an **electrical generator**

front: What is another name for **voltage**?
back: Voltage is also known as **potential difference** (p.d.).

front: The voltage of a source causes a **______** to flow in the circuit.
back: The voltage of a source causes a **current** to flow in the circuit.

front:
**True or False?**

Voltage is measured in amperes.
back:
**False.**

Voltage is measured in **volts** (V).

front: How is voltage shared in a **series circuit**?
back:
In a series circuit, the voltage of the source is **shared** between the components.

The **sum** of the voltages across the individual components is **equal** to the total voltage of the power supply. If the components have **equal resistance**, the voltage is shared **equally**.

front: Define **voltmeter**.
back: A **voltmeter** is a device used to measure the **voltage** (potential difference) between **two points** in a circuit.

front:
**True or False?**

Voltmeters are connected in series with the component being measured.
back:
**False.**

Voltmeters are connected in **parallel** with the component being measured. This is because voltage is the difference in electrical potential between **two points** in a circuit.

front:
**True or False?**

Electromotive force (e.m.f.) is the potential difference of the power source in a circuit. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**True.**

Electromotive force (e.m.f.) is the name given to the **potential difference** of the **power source** in a circuit.

front: Define **electromotive force** (e.m.f.). **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Electromotive force (e.m.f.)** is the electrical **work done** by a source in moving a **unit charge** around a complete circuit. It is measured in **volts (V)**.

front: Define **potential difference**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Potential difference** is the **work done** by a **unit charge** passing between two points in a circuit.

front:
**True or False?**

Potential difference is measured in amperes. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

Potential difference is measured in **volts** (V).

front: As electrons flow through a cell they **______** energy, and as they flow through the components in a circuit they **______** energy. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: As electrons flow through a cell they **gain** energy, and as they flow through the components in a circuit they **lose** energy.

front:
**True or False?**

Resistance is a measure of how difficult it is for current to pass through a conductor or component.
back:
**True.**

**Resistance** is the **opposition to current**. The higher the resistance of a circuit, the lower the current.

front: What is the **equation** for Ohm's law?
back:
The equation for Ohm's law is: $R = \frac{V}{I}$

Where:

- $R$ = resistance, measured in ohms (Ω)
- $V$ = potential difference, measured in volts (V)
- $I$ = current, measured in amperes (A)

front:
**True or False?**

The unit of resistance is volts.
back:
**False.**

The unit of resistance is the **ohm**, represented by the Greek letter omega (Ω).

front: What is an ***I-V*** **graph**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: An *I-V* graph, or **current-voltage graph**, shows the relationship between the **current** flowing through a component and the **potential difference** across it.

front: What is the shape of the *I-V* graph for a wire or fixed **resistor**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The *I-V* graph for a wire or fixed resistor (at constant temperature) is a **straight line** passing through the **origin**. Current is **directly proportional** to potential difference, so the resistance is **constant**. These components are known as **ohmic resistors**.

front:
**True or False?**

The resistance of a non-ohmic resistor is constant. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

A **non-ohmic resistor** has a resistance that is **not constant**, so its *I-V* graph is **not** a straight line.

front: State the independent and dependent variables in the investigation of how the length of a wire affects its resistance.
back:
In this investigation:

- the **independent variable** is the **length** of the resistance wire
- the **dependent variable** is the **resistance** of the wire

front: State two control variables in the investigation of how the length of a wire affects its resistance.
back:
- the **voltage** of the power supply
- the **temperature** of the wire

front: In the resistance investigation, the length of the wire between the crocodile clips is measured using a **______**.
back: In the resistance investigation, the length of the wire between the crocodile clips is measured using a **metre rule**.

front: How is the resistance of each length of wire calculated in the resistance investigation?
back: The resistance of each length of wire is calculated using the equation $R = \frac{V}{I}$, where the voltage *V* is measured using a **voltmeter** and the current *I* is measured using an **ammeter**.

front: Describe the expected graph of resistance against length for a wire at constant temperature.
back: The graph is a **straight line through the origin** with a **positive correlation** — the longer the wire, the higher its resistance.

front:
**True or False?**

The temperature of the wire must be kept constant throughout the resistance investigation.
back:
**True.**

Keeping the temperature of the wire constant ensures its resistance stays constant. This is done by using **low values of current** and switching off the current **between readings**.

front: How can zero errors be avoided in the resistance investigation?
back:
- ensure the first crocodile clip starts at **0** on the metre rule
- ensure the **ammeter** and **voltmeter** both start from zero

front: State one safety precaution that should be taken when investigating the resistance of a wire.
back:
Any one from:

- never touch the wire directly when the circuit is switched on, as it can become very **hot**
- switch off the power supply immediately if burning is smelled
- keep liquids away from the electrical equipment

front: Define the **resistance of a wire**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The resistance of a wire is the opposition to the flow of **electrons** as they pass through the wire, caused by their **collisions** with the **metal ions** in the wire.

front: How does the length of a wire affect its resistance? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The resistance of a wire is **directly proportional** to its length. This means that as the length of the wire increases, its resistance also increases by the same factor.

front: How does the cross-sectional area of a wire affect its resistance? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The resistance of a wire is **inversely proportional** to its cross-sectional area. As the wire's cross-sectional area (thickness) increases, its resistance decreases, and vice versa.

front:
**True or False?**

If a wire is thicker, its resistance is greater. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

If a wire is thicker (greater diameter), there is more space for the electrons to flow through, so its resistance is **smaller**.

front:
**True or False?**

If a wire is longer, its resistance is higher. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**True.**

If a wire is longer, each electron will collide with **more metal ions** along the wire's length, resulting in a greater opposition to the flow of electrons.

front: If the length of a wire is increased by a factor of 3, what is the effect on its resistance? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The resistance of a wire is **directly proportional** to its length, so if the length is increased by a factor of 3, the resistance will also increase by a factor of 3.

front: If the cross-sectional area of a wire is halved, what is the effect on its resistance? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The resistance of a wire is **inversely proportional** to its cross-sectional area, therefore if its cross-sectional area is halved, its resistance will double.

front: Define **electrical energy**.
back:
Electrical energy is the **energy transferred by an electric current**.

It is transferred from a power source to the components in a circuit, where it is transferred to other **stores** of energy, such as thermal or kinetic stores.

front:
**True or False?**

The energy transferred in a circuit is related to potential difference, current and time.
back:
**True.**

The energy transferred is related to potential difference, current and time, as described by the equation $E = V \times I \times t$.

front: What is the electrical energy equation?
back:
The electrical energy equation is $E = V \times I \times t$, where:

- $E$ = energy transferred, measured in joules (J)
- $V$ = potential difference, measured in volts (V)
- $I$ = current, measured in amps (A)
- $t$ = time, measured in seconds (s)

front: How is energy transferred in a circuit?
back:
Energy is transferred from the power source to the components connected in the circuit:

- as charge passes through the **power supply**, energy is transferred **to the charge**
- as the charge passes through each **component**, energy is transferred from the charge to the component

front: What two factors affect the amount of energy transferred by an electrical appliance?
back:
The amount of energy transferred by an electrical appliance depends on:

- how **long** the appliance runs for
- the **power rating** of the appliance

front:
**True or False?**

Energy in a circuit is transferred from the power source to the components and the surroundings.
back:
**True.**

Energy is transferred from the power source to the components, which often **dissipate** some of that energy to the surroundings.

front: What is the main energy transfer in a toaster while it toasts a slice of bread?
back: Energy is transferred **electrically** from the mains supply to the **thermal store** of the heating element, which heats up the bread.

front: What is the main energy transfer in a washing machine during a washing cycle?
back: Energy is transferred **electrically** from the mains supply to the **kinetic store** of the motor, which rotates the drum.

front: Define **electrical power**.
back: Electrical power is the **rate** at which energy is transferred by an appliance. It is measured in watts (W).

front:
**True or False?**

Power is the rate of doing work.
back:
**True.**

Power is defined as the rate of doing work, or the rate of energy transfer. It is measured in watts (W).

front: What is the electrical power equation?
back:
The electrical power equation is $P = I \times V$, where:

- $P$ = power, measured in watts (W)
- $I$ = current, measured in amps (A)
- $V$ = potential difference, measured in volts (V)

front: State the equation for power in terms of work done.
back:
The equation for power in terms of work done is $P = \frac{W}{t}$, where:

- $P$ = power, measured in watts (W)
- $W$ = work done, which is equivalent to energy transferred, measured in joules (J)
- $t$ = time, measured in seconds (s)

front:
**True or False?**

The unit of power is joules (J).
back:
**False.**

The unit of power is watts (W), where 1 watt is equivalent to 1 joule per second (J/s).

front:
**True or False?**

Energy usage in homes is measured in joules (J).
back:
The kilowatt-hour (kW h) is a **unit of energy**. It is the energy transferred by 1 kilowatt of power used for 1 hour.

It is mostly used to measure energy usage in homes, businesses and factories.

front:
**True or False?**

Energy usage in homes is measured in joules (J).
back:
**False.**

Energy usage in homes is commonly measured in **kilowatt-hours** (kW h), because the energy transferred by household appliances measured in joules would be an inconveniently large number.

front: What is the equation for energy transferred in kilowatt-hours (kW h)?
back:
The equation for energy transferred in kilowatt-hours is $E = P \times t$, where:

- $E$ = energy transferred, measured in kilowatt-hours (kW h)
- $P$ = power, measured in kilowatts (kW)
- $t$ = time, measured in hours (h)

front: How many joules are there in 1 kilowatt-hour (kW h)?
back:
There are $3 . 6 \times 10^{6}$ joules in 1 kilowatt-hour:

$1 \text{kW h} = 1000 \text{W} \times 3600 \text{s} = 3 . 6 \times 10^{6} \text{J}$

front: What is the difference between the circuit symbols for a **fixed resistor** and a **variable resistor**?
back:
The symbol for a **variable resistor** has an **arrow** going through it, whereas the symbol for a **fixed resistor** does not.

The resistance of a variable resistor can be **adjusted**, but the resistance of a fixed resistor is **constant**.

front: How should an **ammeter** and a **voltmeter** be connected in a circuit?
back:
**Ammeters** are always connected in **series**.

**Voltmeters** are always connected in **parallel**.

front: What is the function of a **fuse** in a circuit?
back: A **fuse** protects expensive components from **current surges** and acts as a safety measure against **fire**.

front: Name **three** functional components and state what each does when current passes through it.
back:
- **Motors** rotate
- **Lamps** emit light
- **Heaters** transfer thermal energy

front: Define **generator**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
A **generator** is a device which produces **current**.

A **d.c. generator** is a source of **direct current** and an **a.c. generator** is a source of **alternating current**.

front: In which direction does current flow through a **diode**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
Current can only flow through a diode in **one direction**.

This is the direction that the **triangle** points in the circuit symbol.

front: Why can an **LED** be used to indicate the presence of a current in a circuit? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: An **LED** illuminates when current flows through it in the correct direction, so it gives a **visual response** to the presence of a current.

front:
**True or False?**

Current is different at different points in a series circuit.
back:
**False.**

Current is the **same** value at any point in a series circuit.

front:
**True or False?**

The amount of current flowing in a series circuit depends on the voltage of the power source and the resistance of the components in the circuit.
back:
**True.**

The amount of current flowing in a series circuit depends on the **voltage** of the power source and the **resistance** of the components in the circuit.

front: If the voltage of the power source is increased, but everything else in the circuit remains constant, what effect does this have on the **current**?
back: If the **voltage** of the power source is increased, but everything else in the circuit remains constant, **more current** is driven around the circuit, so the current will **increase**.

front: If the voltage of the power source remains constant, but more components are added to the circuit, what effect does this have on the **current**?
back: Adding components to the circuit increases the **total resistance** of the circuit, so the current will **decrease** (for a constant voltage).

front:
**True or False?**

In a parallel circuit, the current from the power source is larger than the current in each branch.
back:
**True.**

The current **splits** along each **branch** at a junction, so the current from the source is **larger** than the current in each branch.

front:
**True or False?**

One advantage of a parallel circuit is that each lamp can be arranged in its own branch with its own switch.
back:
**True.**

In a parallel circuit, lamps can be switched off and on **individually** without breaking the whole circuit.

front:
**True or False?**

One advantage of a series circuit is that if one component stops working the others will still work.
back:
**False.**

An advantage of **parallel** circuits is that if one bulb breaks, the rest continue to function, as current passes along each branch independently.

If one component fails in a **series** circuit, then the circuit is broken and the current cannot flow.

front:
**True or False?**

Current is conserved at a junction in a parallel circuit. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**True.**

The current flowing into the junction is equal to the current flowing out of it.

This is because **charge** is conserved.

front:
**True or False?**

Current always splits equally at a junction in a parallel circuit. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

Current will only split equally at a junction if the **resistance** of the components along each branch is **identical**.

front: What is the rule for potential difference in a series circuit? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: In a series circuit, the **sum** of the potential differences across the components is equal to the **total e.m.f.** of the power supply.

front: What is the rule for potential difference in a parallel circuit? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The potential difference across **each branch** of a parallel circuit is the **same** as the e.m.f. of the power source.

front: If one branch of a parallel circuit contains multiple components, what happens to the potential difference across that branch? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The potential difference across the branch is **split** between the components on that branch.

front: What is the rule for calculating the combined resistance of two or more components in series?
back: When two or more components are connected in **series**, the **combined resistance** is equal to the **sum** of the **individual resistances**.

front:
**True or False?**

The combined resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than that of either resistor by itself.
back:
**True.**

When resistors are connected in **parallel**, the combined resistance is **less than** the resistance of any of the individual components.

front:
**True or False?**

If two resistors of equal resistance are connected in parallel, the combined resistance will halve.
back:
**True.**

If two resistors of equal resistance are connected in parallel, the combined resistance is **half** the value of each individual resistor.

front: State the equation for calculating the combined resistance of two resistors connected in parallel. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The equation for the combined resistance of two resistors connected in parallel is

$\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_{1}} + \frac{1}{R_{2}}$

Where:

- $R$ = the combined resistance, measured in ohms (Ω)
- $R_{1}$ = the resistance of resistor 1, measured in ohms (Ω)
- $R_{2}$ = the resistance of resistor 2, measured in ohms (Ω)

front: Why does a resistor heat up when an electric current passes through it?
back: When a current passes through a **resistor**, energy is transferred to **heat** due to the **collisions of the free electrons** within it, so its **temperature increases**. Some of this energy is dissipated into the surroundings by heating.

front: What hazard does damaged insulation on a wire pose?
back: Exposed wires can cause **electric shocks** if touched.

front: What hazard does the overheating of cables pose?
back: Overheating of cables could cause the insulation to **melt**, or even cause a **fire**.

front: Why is it dangerous to use electrical circuits in damp conditions?
back: Water is an **electrical conductor**, so moisture touching a live wire could set up a **short circuit** within the device (which could cause a fire) or a **conductive path** for current to flow through a person to the earth, causing **electrocution**.

front: Why is it dangerous to overload plugs, extension leads and multiple sockets when using the mains supply?
back: Overloading the mains supply can cause an **excessive current** to flow. The heat created could cause the insulation to **melt**, or even cause a **fire**.

front: Name **four** safety features built into domestic electrical appliances.
back:
Safety features built into domestic appliances include:

- **double insulation**
- **earthing**
- **fuses**
- **circuit breakers** (trip switches)

front: What does it mean for an appliance to be **double insulated**?
back:
A **double insulated** appliance has two layers of insulation:

- **insulation** around the wires themselves
- a **non-metallic case** that acts as a second layer of insulation

Double insulated appliances do not require an **earth wire**.

front: Why does the casing of an electrical appliance have to be either non-conducting or earthed?
back: The casing of an electrical appliance must be either non-conducting or earthed to **prevent** the casing from becoming electrified and causing an **electric shock** to anyone who touches it.

front: How does the **earth wire** make an appliance safe if a live wire touches its metal case?
back: The earth wire provides a **low resistance path to the earth**. This causes a **surge of current** in the earth wire and hence also in the live wire. The high current causes the fuse to **melt and break**, which **cuts off the supply of electricity** to the appliance, making it safe.

front: What is the purpose of a fuse?
back: A **fuse** is a safety device designed to **cut off the flow of electricity** to an individual appliance if the current becomes **too large** due to a fault or a surge.

front: How does a **fuse** stop the current when the current becomes too large?
back: The thin metal **wire** inside the fuse **heats up** and **melts**. This causes the wire to **break**, breaking the **circuit** and **stopping the current**.

front: How do you choose the correct **fuse rating** for an appliance?
back: Choose the fuse with the value **just above** the current required by the appliance. Fuses come in values of **3 A**, **5 A** and **13 A**, so an appliance using 3.1 A needs a **5 A** fuse.

front:
**True or False?**

A fuse without an earth wire protects the circuit and the cabling for a double-insulated appliance.
back:
**True.**

A double-insulated appliance does not require an **earth wire**, but a fuse still protects the **circuit** and the **cabling** from excess current.

front: What is the function of a trip switch?
back: A **trip switch** is a switch on the **consumer unit** that automatically **breaks the circuit** if the current becomes too high.

front: What are the main **advantages** of trip switches?
back: Trip switches provide protection from **current surges or faults**, and they can be **reset** when the problem is fixed.

front: Fuses are located in the **______**, while trip switches are located in the **______**.
back: Fuses are located in the **plug**, while trip switches are located in the **consumer unit**.

front: What is **electromagnetic induction**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Electromagnetic induction** is the effect where an **e.m.f. is induced** in a conductor whenever there is **relative movement** between the conductor and a **magnetic field**.

front: How can an e.m.f. be induced in a wire? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: An e.m.f. can be induced in a wire by moving it through a magnetic field, so that the wire **cuts** the magnetic field lines.

front:
**True or False?**

An e.m.f. can only be induced by moving a conductor in a magnetic field. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

An e.m.f. can also be induced by placing a stationary conductor in a **changing** magnetic field.

front: What **apparatus** can be used to determine if an e.m.f. has been induced in a conductor? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
A **sensitive voltmeter** can be used to measure the size of the induced e.m.f.

If the conductor is part of a **complete circuit**, the induced **current** can be detected by an **ammeter**.

front:
**True or False?**

An e.m.f. is induced when a coil and a bar magnet move in the same direction at the same speed. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

For electromagnetic induction to occur, there must be **relative movement** between the conductor and the magnetic field.

Therefore, an e.m.f. is **not** induced when a coil and a bar magnet move in the same direction at the same speed.

front: What **four** factors affect the **size** of an induced e.m.f.? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The four factors that affect the size of an induced e.m.f. are:

- the **speed** at which the wire, coil or magnet is moved
- the **number of turns** on the coils in the wire
- the **size** of the coils
- the **strength** of the magnetic field

front: How can the **direction** of an induced e.m.f. be reversed? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The direction of an induced e.m.f. can be reversed by:

- reversing the **direction** in which the wire, coil or magnet is moved
- switching the **poles** of the magnet

front: Define **a.c. generator**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: An **a.c. generator** is a device which converts energy from **motion** into an **electrical** output.

front: What is the **output** of an a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: An a.c. generator produces an **alternating e.m.f.**, which causes an **alternating current** to flow.

front: What components make up a simple a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
A simple a.c. generator consists of:

- a **rotating coil** of wire between the poles of a **permanent magnet**
- **slip rings** and **brushes** connected to an external circuit

front: What is the purpose of the **slip rings** in an a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The purpose of the slip rings is to allow the **alternating current** to flow between the **rotating coil** and the **external circuit**.

front:
**True or False?**

A maximum e.m.f. is induced in an a.c. generator when the coil is moving parallel to the magnetic field. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

A maximum e.m.f. is induced when the coil is in a **horizontal** position and its motion is **perpendicular** to the field.

This is because the greatest number of field lines are cut when the coil moves perpendicular to the field.

front:
**True or False?**

There is a point in the rotation of an a.c. generator's coil where no e.m.f. is induced. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**True.**

No e.m.f. is induced when the coil is in a **vertical** position and its motion is **parallel** to the field.

This is because no field lines are cut when the coil moves parallel to the field.

front: How often does the direction of the induced e.m.f. reverse as the coil of an a.c. generator rotates? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The direction of the induced e.m.f. (and current) reverses every **half rotation** of the coil.

front: What is the shape of the graph of e.m.f. against time for an a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The graph of e.m.f. against time for an a.c. generator is a **sine** or **cosine** curve, depending on the starting position of the coil:

- starting from a **horizontal** position (maximum e.m.f.), the graph is a **cosine** curve
- starting from a **vertical** position (zero e.m.f.), the graph is a **sine** curve

front: How can the size of the induced e.m.f. be **increased** in an a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
In an a.c. generator, the size of the induced e.m.f. can be increased by:

- increasing the **frequency** of rotation of the coil
- increasing the number of **turns** on the coil
- increasing the **strength** of the magnet
- inserting a **soft iron core** into the coil

front: What is the pattern of the magnetic field due to the current in a straight wire? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The magnetic field due to a current in a straight wire forms **concentric circles** centred on the wire, which get **further apart** with increasing distance from the wire.

front:
**True or False?**

The magnetic field around a current-carrying straight wire has no poles. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**True.**

The **circular** field pattern around a current-carrying wire indicates that the field has **no poles**.

front: What rule is used to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The **right-hand grip rule** is used to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire.

Point the **right-hand thumb** in the direction of the (conventional) current; the direction of the **curled fingers** represents the direction of the magnetic field lines.

front: What is the pattern of the magnetic field around a current-carrying solenoid? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The field lines around a solenoid are similar to those of a **bar magnet**:

- one end of the solenoid becomes a **north** pole and the other a **south** pole
- the field lines **emerge** from the north pole and **return** to the south pole

front:
**True or False?**

When viewed from the end of a solenoid, the pole is a north pole if the current travels clockwise around the coil. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

The **north** pole forms at the end where the current flows **anticlockwise**, and the **south** pole at the end where the current flows **clockwise**.

front: How can the **strength** of the magnetic field around a straight wire be increased? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The strength of the magnetic field around a straight wire can be increased by increasing the amount of **current** flowing through the wire.

The field is **strongest near the wire** and becomes weaker further away, shown by the field lines becoming **further apart**.

front: How can the **strength** of the magnetic field around a solenoid be increased? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The strength of the magnetic field around a solenoid can be increased by:

- increasing the amount of **current** flowing through the coil
- increasing the **number of turns** on the coil
- inserting an **iron core** into the coil

front: What effect does reversing the current have on the magnetic field around a wire or solenoid? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Reversing the direction of the **current** reverses the **direction** of the magnetic field produced.

front: Why does inserting a **soft iron core** into a solenoid produce a stronger magnet? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The iron core becomes an **induced magnet** when a current flows through the coils.

The magnetic field produced by the solenoid and the iron core together creates a much **stronger** magnet overall — this is how an **electromagnet** works.

front: Why does a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experience a force? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
A current-carrying conductor produces its **own magnetic field**.

When this interacts with an **external magnetic field**, the conductor experiences a **force**, which makes it move.

front:
**True or False?**

A current-carrying conductor will only experience a force if the current is parallel to the magnetic field lines. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

A current-carrying conductor will only experience a force if the current through it is **perpendicular** to the direction of the magnetic field lines.

front: How can the direction of the **force** on a current-carrying conductor be reversed? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor can be reversed by:

- reversing the direction of the **current**
- reversing the direction of the **magnetic field**

front: What is **Fleming's left-hand rule** used for? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Fleming's left-hand rule is used to determine the direction of the **force** (thrust) on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, given the directions of the **current** and the **magnetic field**.

front: State the quantity represented by each finger in Fleming's left-hand rule. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
In Fleming's left-hand rule:

- the **thumb** points in the direction of the **force** (thrust) on the conductor
- the **first finger** points in the direction of the **magnetic field**
- the **second finger** points in the direction of the **current** (from positive to negative)

front:
**True or False?**

The direction of the force on a current-carrying wire depends on the direction of the current and the magnetic field. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**True.**

The direction of the force on a current-carrying wire depends on the direction of the **current** and the direction of the **magnetic field**.

In Fleming's left-hand rule, the force, field and current are all **perpendicular** to each other.

front: What can the **motor effect** be used to create? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The motor effect can be used to create a simple **d.c. electric motor**.

The force on a current-carrying coil causes it to **rotate** in a single direction.

front: Describe the structure of a simple **d.c. motor**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
A simple d.c. motor consists of:

- a **coil of wire** (which is free to rotate) between the poles of a **permanent magnet**
- a **split-ring commutator** and **brushes** connected to a source of d.c.

front: What causes the **coil** in a d.c. motor to **rotate**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
As current flows through the coil, it produces a magnetic field which interacts with the external magnetic field.

Forces act in **opposite directions** on each side of the coil, causing a **turning effect**.

front: What does the **split-ring commutator** do to the current in a d.c. motor? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The split-ring commutator **reverses** the direction of the current in the coil every **half turn**, so the forces on the coil continue to cause rotation in the **same direction**.

front:
**True or False?**

When the coil of a d.c. motor is in the vertical position, no force acts on it. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**True.**

When the coil is vertical, the split ring is **no longer in contact** with the brushes, so no current flows and no forces act.

The **momentum** of the coil causes it to continue rotating until the split ring reconnects with the brushes.

front: What factors affect the **speed** of rotation of a d.c. motor? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The speed at which the coil of a d.c. motor rotates can be increased by:

- increasing the **current**
- using a **stronger magnet**

front: How can the **direction of rotation** of the coil in a d.c. motor be changed? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The direction of rotation of the coil in a d.c. motor can be changed by:

- reversing the direction of the **current supply**
- reversing the direction of the magnetic field by reversing the **poles** of the magnet

front: How can the **force** supplied by a d.c. motor be increased? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The force supplied by a d.c. motor can be increased by:

- increasing the **current** in the coil
- increasing the strength of the **magnetic field**
- adding **more turns** to the coil

front: How can you determine the **direction of rotation** of the coil in a d.c. motor? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
To determine the direction of rotation of the coil in a d.c. motor:

- draw arrows for the direction of the **magnetic field** (north to south) and the **current** (positive to negative)
- use **Fleming's left-hand rule** to find the direction of the force on each side of the coil
- use the force directions to determine the direction of rotation

front: What is the **function** of a transformer? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
A **transformer** is a device used to **change** the size of an **alternating voltage** or current.

This is achieved using the generator effect.

front: Describe the **structure** of a simple transformer. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
A basic transformer consists of:

- a **primary coil**
- a **secondary coil**
- a **soft iron core**

front: Why is the core of a transformer made from **soft iron**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Iron is used for the core of a transformer because it is easily **magnetised**.

front: What is a **step-up** transformer? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
A **step-up** transformer:

- **increases** the voltage of a power source `\left(V_{s} > V_{p}\right)`
- has **more turns** on the secondary coil than on the primary coil `\left(N_{s} > N_{p}\right)`

front:
**True or False?**

A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the primary coil than the secondary coil. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

A **step-down** transformer has **fewer turns** on the **secondary** coil than on the primary coil `\left(N_{s} < N_{p}\right)`.

This **decreases** the voltage of the power source `\left(V_{s} < V_{p}\right)`.

front:
State the type of transformer in the diagram. **(Extended Tier Only)**

![A transformer with primary voltage labelled 300V on the left side and secondary voltage labelled 180V on the right side, connected by coils.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-Flashcards/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-physics/electricity-and-magnetism/electromagnetic-effects/assets/e784b78bd33a-23569-transformer-example.bin)
back:
The transformer in the diagram is a **step-down** transformer.

The secondary voltage (180 V) is **lower** than the primary voltage (300 V).

front: State the **transformer equation**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The ratio of the voltages across the primary and secondary coils of a transformer is equal to the ratio of the number of turns on each coil:

$\frac{V_{p}}{V_{s}} = \frac{N_{p}}{N_{s}}$

Where:

- $V_{p}$ = voltage across the primary coil, in volts (V)
- $V_{s}$ = voltage across the secondary coil, in volts (V)
- $N_{p}$ = number of turns on the primary coil
- $N_{s}$ = number of turns on the secondary coil

front: How is the **output (secondary) voltage** of a transformer calculated? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The output (secondary) voltage of a transformer is calculated using:

$V_{s} = V_{p} \times \frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}$

This shows that the output voltage depends on:

- the **number of turns** on the primary and secondary coils
- the input (**primary**) voltage

front: Define **ideal transformer**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: An **ideal transformer** is a transformer which is **100% efficient**, so the input power in the primary coil is equal to the output power of the secondary coil.

front: State the equation for an **ideal transformer**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The equation for an ideal transformer is:

$I_{p} V_{p} = I_{s} V_{s}$

Where:

- $I_{p}$ = primary current, in amps (A)
- $V_{p}$ = primary voltage, in volts (V)
- $I_{s}$ = secondary current, in amps (A)
- $V_{s}$ = secondary voltage, in volts (V)

front:
**True or False?**

A transformer can increase both the voltage and the power output of a power source. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

Although transformers can increase the **voltage** of a power source, due to the law of **conservation of energy**, they cannot increase the **power** output.

front: Why is electricity transmitted at **high voltage**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
Since $P = V I$, a high voltage means electricity can be transmitted at a **low current**.

A smaller current flowing through the power lines results in **less heat** being produced due to resistance in the wire.

This **reduces** the **energy loss** in the power lines, making the energy transfer more efficient.

front: State the equation for the **power dissipated** in a wire due to resistance. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The power dissipated in a wire due to resistance is given by:

$P = I^{2} R$

Where:

- *P* = power, in watts (W)
- *I* = current, in amps (A)
- *R* = resistance, in ohms (Ω)

front: Where are **step-up** and **step-down** transformers used in high-voltage transmission? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
A **step-up** transformer is used to increase the voltage and decrease the current of electricity **before** transmission.

This ensures the same power transfer with a smaller current, so less thermal energy is lost due to resistance in the wire.

A **step-down** transformer is used to decrease the voltage and increase the current of electricity **after** transmission, because high-voltage electricity is dangerous for use in homes.

front: What is a **ruler**?
back: A ruler is an instrument used to measure **small distances** of a **few centimetres**.

front:
**True or False?**

Rulers measure to the nearest millimetre.
back:
**True.**

Rulers measure to the nearest millimetre.

front: What is the purpose of a **tape measure**?
back: A **tape measure** is appropriate for measuring distances of a **few metres**.

front: Which device can be used to measure distances of up to a kilometre?
back: A **trundle wheel** is used to measure large distances up to a kilometre.

front: What is a **measuring cylinder**?
back: A measuring cylinder is a device used to measure the **volume of liquids**.

front: What device can be used to measure **time intervals**?
back: A stopwatch can be used to measure **time** intervals.

front: Define the term **reaction time**.
back: Reaction time is how **long** it takes someone to react to an event.

front:
**True or False?**

Human reaction time has **more** of an impact on **short-time** measurements than long-time measurements.
back:
**True.**

Human reaction time has more of an impact on **short-time** measurements than long-time measurements.

front: State the equation for calculating an average.
back: The equation for calculating an average is $\mathrm{average}=\frac{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{value}}{\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{values}}$

front: What is the purpose of taking **multiple readings** in physics experiments?
back: The purpose of taking **multiple readings** in physics experiments is to obtain an **accurate** measurement value.

front: A measuring cylinder can be used to find the volume of an irregularly shaped solid by measuring the **______** in volume.
back: A measuring cylinder can be used to find the volume of an irregularly shaped solid by measuring the **change** in volume.

front: Define a scalar quantity. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: A scalar quantity is a quantity that has only **magnitude**.

front: What is a vector quantity?  **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: A vector quantity is a quantity that has both **magnitude and direction**.

front: What is displacement?  **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The distance from a **starting point**.

front:
**True or False?**

Mass is a scalar quantity.
back:
**True.**

Mass is a** scalar quantity** as it has only magnitude.

front:
**True or False?**

Distance is a scalar quantity.
back:
**True.**

Distance is a scalar quantity.

front: How can you determine whether a quantity is a scalar or vector? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Determine if it has only **magnitude** (scalar) or magnitude and **direction** (vector).

front: Is 100 km due north a scalar or a vector quantity? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: 100 km due north is a vector quantity because it includes both a magnitude and a direction.

front:
**True or False?**

Energy is a scalar.
back:
**True**

Energy is a scalar.

front: Is temperature a scalar or a vector?  **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Temperature is a **scalar**.

front: Is electric field strength a scalar or a vector? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Electric field strength is a **vector**.

front: What is speed?
back: Speed is the **distance travelled per unit time**.

front:
**True or False?**

Speed is a vector quantity.
back:
**False. **

Speed is a **scalar** quantity because it only contains magnitude.

front: Define** average speed**.
back: Average speed is the **total distance** travelled **divided** by the **total time** taken.

front: State the equation for calculating **average speed**.
back: The equation for calculating average speed is $\mathrm{Average} \mathrm{speed}=\frac{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled}}{\mathrm{time} \mathrm{taken}}$

front: What does velocity describe that speed does not?
back: Velocity describes both **magnitude and direction** of motion whereas speed describes only magnitude.

front: Define **velocity**.
back: Velocity is defined as the **rate of change of displacement** with respect to time.

front: What is the equation for calculating velocity?
back:
The equation for velocity is $v=\frac{s}{t}$

Where:

- $v$ = velocity, measured in metres per second (m/s)
- $s$ = displacement, measured in metres (m)
- $t$ = time, measured in seconds (s)

front:
**True or False?**

Velocity is a scalar quantity.
back:
**False. **

Velocity is a **vector **quantity because it includes **direction**.

front: What units are used to measure speed and velocity?
back: Both speed and velocity are measured in metres per second (m/s).

front: What is the significance of negative velocity values?
back: The significance of negative velocity values indicates motion in the opposite direction.

front: How is displacement different from distance in calculating velocity?
back: Displacement is different from distance in calculating velocity because it accounts for direction.

front: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
back: The difference between speed and velocity is that speed is a **scalar**, while velocity is a **vector** as it includes direction.

front: How do you calculate the total distance from the average speed?
back: The total distance is calculated from the average speed by **multiplying** the average speed by the total time taken.

front: What is the difference between **acceleration** and **deceleration**?
back: An object is **accelerating** when it is **speeding up** and **decelerating** when it is **slowing down**.

front: Define **acceleration**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Acceleration** is the **rate of change of velocity**.

front: State the equation for calculating **acceleration**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The equation for **acceleration** is:

$a = \frac{Δv}{Δt}$

Where:

- $a$ = acceleration, measured in metres per second squared (m/s²)
- $Δ v$ = change in velocity, measured in metres per second (m/s)
- $Δ t$ = time taken, measured in seconds (s)

front: How do you find the **change in velocity**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The **change in velocity** is the **final velocity** minus the **initial velocity**:

$Δ v = v - u$

front: What units are used to measure **acceleration**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Acceleration** is measured in **metres per second squared (m/s²)**.

front: What does a **positive acceleration** indicate? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: A **positive acceleration** indicates that the object is **speeding up**.

front:
**True or False?**

Deceleration is a negative acceleration.
back:
**True.**

A **decelerating** object is **slowing down**, so its **acceleration is negative**.

front: Which type of graph shows the distance travelled by a moving object over a period of time?
back: A **distance-time** graph shows the distance travelled by a moving object over a period of time.

front: How is constant speed represented on a distance-time graph?
back:
On a distance time graph, constant speed is represented by a **straight line**:

- a steeper slope shows a greater constant speed
- a shallower slope shows a lower constant speed
- a flat, horizontal line shows a constant speed of zero

front: How is changing speed represented on a distance-time graph?
back: On a distance-time graph, changing speed is represented by a **curved line**.

front: State the equation used to find the gradient of a **distance-time graph**.
back:
The equation used to find the gradient of a distance-time graph is $\mathrm{speed}=\mathrm{gradient}=\frac{\Deltay}{\Deltax}$

Where:

- $\Deltay$ = change in distance
- $\Deltax$ = change in time

**True or False?**

front: What does a **speed-time** graph show?
back: A speed-time graph shows how the **speed **of a moving object varies with** time**.

front: What is **constant acceleration** on a speed-time graph?
back: Constant acceleration on a speed-time graph is represented by a** straight**,** sloping line**.

front:
**True or False?**

A **gentle slope** on a speed-time graph represents large acceleration.
back:
**False.**

A **gentle slope** on a speed-time graph represents a small acceleration.

front: Describe the motion shown in this speed-time graph.\n\n![Speed-time graph showing a curved line that starts at the origin, curves upward steeply, and then flattens out.](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/07/8121_speed-time-graph-decreasing-acceleration){width=386 height=288}
back:
The speed-time graph shows** decreasing acceleration**.

The change in speed per unit time decreases.

![Speed-time graph showing a curved line that starts at the origin, curves upward steeply, and then flattens out.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-Flashcards/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-physics/motion-forces-and-energy/motion/assets/5f18bdeb2965-59470-speed-time-graph-decreasing-acceleration.bin)

front: What does a **flat**,** horizontal line** represent on a speed-time graph?
back: A flat, horizontal line indicates that the **acceleration is zero**, meaning the object is moving at a constant speed.

front: What does the **area** under a speed-time graph represent?
back: The area under a speed-time graph represents the **distance** travelled by the object.

front: How do you calculate the **total area** under a speed-time graph?
back: The total area under a speed-time graph shows the total distance travelled. The total area is the sum of the areas of each enclosed section (triangle or rectangle).

front: What is the** formula** to calculate the area of a triangle?
back:
The formula to calculate the area of a triangle is $A=\frac{1}{2}\timesb\timesh$

Where:

- $b$ = base of triangle, measured in metres (m) or centimetres (cm)
- $h$ = height of triangle, measured in metres (m) or centimetres (cm)

front: What is the formula to calculate the** area** of a **rectangle**?
back:
The formula to calculate the area of a rectangle is $A=b\timesh$

Where:

- $b$ = base of rectangle, measured in metres (m) or centimetres (cm)

- $h$ = height of rectangle, measured in metres (m) or centimetres (cm)

front: What **shape** does the area beneath a speed-time graph form for an object with **constant speed**?
back: The area under a speed-time graph forms  a **rectangle**.

front:
**True or False?**

A **flat line** on a speed-time graph indicates constant acceleration.
back:
**False.**

A flat line on a speed-time graph indicates **constant speed**.

**True or False?**

The starting speed of this object is zero.
