back:
**False. **

The starting speed is not zero because the line does not start from the origin.

![Speed-time graph showing a straight line sloping upward. The line begins at t= 0 where speed is not equal to zero. ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-Flashcards/cie-igcse-science-co-ordinated-sciences-double-award-23-physics/motion-forces-and-energy/motion/assets/423f3f47b59c-45865-speed-time-graph-constant-acceleration-non.bin)

front: What does the **gradient** of a speed-time graph represent? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The **gradient** of a speed-time graph represents the **acceleration** of the object.

front: What do a **positive** and a **negative gradient** indicate on a speed-time graph? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: A **positive gradient** shows the object is **accelerating** (speeding up); a **negative gradient** shows the object is **decelerating** (slowing down).

front: How does a speed-time graph show **constant** acceleration compared with **changing** acceleration? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Constant acceleration** is shown by a **straight line**, while **changing acceleration** is shown by a **curve**.

front:
**True or False?**

A curved speed-time graph shows constant acceleration.
back:
**False.**

A **curve** shows **changing acceleration**; a **straight line** shows constant acceleration.

front: On a curved speed-time graph, how can you tell if the acceleration is **increasing** or **decreasing**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: If the curve becomes **steeper** (gradient increasing), the acceleration is **increasing**. If the curve becomes **shallower** (gradient decreasing), the acceleration is **decreasing**.

front: How do you calculate the **acceleration** from a straight-line speed-time graph? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The **acceleration** is the **gradient** of the line:

$a = \frac{Δv}{Δt} = \frac{Δy}{Δx}$

Where:

- $Δ v$ = change in speed
- $Δ t$ = change in time

front: How do you find the **acceleration** at a point on a **curved** speed-time graph? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Draw a **tangent** to the curve at that point and find its **gradient**. This gives the **instantaneous acceleration** at that moment.

front: Define **acceleration of free fall**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Acceleration of free fall** (**g**) is the **acceleration** of an object falling **freely under gravity**, in the **absence of air resistance**.

front: What is the value of the **acceleration of free fall**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The **acceleration of free fall** is *g* = **9.8 m/s²** near the Earth's surface.

front:
**True or False?**

The acceleration of free fall is the same for all objects, regardless of mass.
back:
**True.**

In the **absence of air resistance**, all objects fall with the **same acceleration**, regardless of their mass.

front:
**True or False?**

All objects fall with the same acceleration in the presence of air resistance.
back:
**False.**

With **air resistance**, different objects fall at different accelerations. We usually assume air resistance is **negligible**.

front: Ignoring air resistance, by how much does a falling object's velocity increase each second? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Its velocity increases by **9.8 m/s** every second.

front: Define **mass**.
back: Mass is a measure of the **quantity of matter** in an object.

front:
**True or False?**

Mass is a **vector** quantity.
back:
**False.**

Mass is a **scalar** quantity.

front: The SI unit for mass is **kg**. What does **kg** stand for?
back: The unit **kg** stands for **kilograms**.

front: Define **weight** in terms of the effect of a gravitational field. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Weight is the effect of a **gravitational field** on an object with mass.

front: Define **gravitational field strength**.
back: Gravitational field strength is the **force per unit mass** acting on an object in a gravitational field.

front:
**True or False?**

Weight is a measure of the **quantity of matter** in an object.
back:
**False.**

Weight is a gravitational **force**; it is a **vector** quantity measured in **newtons (N)**.

front:
**True or False?**

An object's mass varies depending on the **gravitational field strength**.
back:
**False.**

An object's mass is **independent** of gravitational field strength; it stays the same everywhere in the Universe.

front: How is an object's **weight** affected by the **gravitational field strength**?
back: The **stronger** the gravitational field strength, the **greater** the object's weight.

front: What is the equation for **gravitational field strength**?
back:
$g = \frac{W}{m}$

Where:

- *g* = gravitational field strength in N/kg
- *W* = weight in N
- *m* = mass in kg

On Earth, *g* = 9.8 N/kg.

front: Define **density**.
back: Density is defined as the **mass per unit volume** of a material. It describes how much mass is contained in a given volume.

front:
**True or False?**

Objects made from **high-density** materials typically have low **mass**.
back:
**False.**

Objects made from high-density materials typically have a high mass.

front: What is the equation for the **density** of an object?
back:
The equation for density is $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$

Where:

- *ρ*  = density, measured in kg / m<sup>3</sup>
- $m$ = mass, measured in kilograms (kg)
- $V$ = volume, measured in metres cubed (m<sup>3</sup>)

front: State the units for density when mass is in grams (**g**) and volume is in cubic centimetres (**cm³**).
back: The units for density are **grams per cubic centimetre** (g/cm³) when mass is measured in grams (g) and volume in cubic centimetres (cm³).

front: Why are gases generally less dense than solids?
back: Gases are generally **less dense** than solids because the molecules in a gas are more spread out over a larger volume.

front:
**True or False?**

Density is a **scalar** quantity.
back:
**True.**

Density is a scalar quantity.

front: Define **volume**.
back: Volume is the amount of **space occupied** by an object in three-dimensional space.

front: State the equation used to calculate the **volume** of an object.
back:
The equation used to calculate the volume of an object is $V=l\timesw\timesh$

Where:

- $l$ = length of object, measured in metres (m)
- $w$ = width of object, measured in metres (m)
- $h$ = height of object, measured in (m)

front: Identify which object is more dense, the one on the left or the one on the right.\n\n![Two cubes with pink spheres inside; the left cube has 4 spread-out spheres, and the right cube is filled with 14 closely packed spheres.](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/07/4782_density-comparrison){width=1100 height=301}
back: The object on the right is more dense because the particles are packed more closely together.

front: How do you measure the **density** of a regularly shaped object?
back:
Measure its **mass** using a **digital balance**, and measure its **dimensions** using a ruler, Vernier calipers or micrometer.

Calculate its **volume** from its shape, then find the density using:

$ρ = \frac{m}{V}$

front: How do you measure the **density** of an irregularly shaped object?
back:
Measure its **mass** using a **digital balance**.

Lower it into a **displacement (eureka) can** and collect the overflowing water in a **measuring cylinder**. Measure the volume of this water, then find the density using:

$ρ = \frac{m}{V}$

front: When an irregular object is fully submerged, the volume of water it **______** is equal to the volume of the object.
back: When an irregular object is fully submerged, the volume of water it **displaces** is equal to the volume of the object.

front: When measuring the density of a liquid, how do you find the **mass of the liquid**?
back:
Subtract the mass of the **empty measuring cylinder** from the mass of the **cylinder with the liquid** in it.

**Mass of liquid = mass of cylinder with liquid − mass of empty cylinder**

front: Which instrument would you use to measure the dimensions of a **very small** object most accurately?
back:
A **micrometer**, which measures objects around 3 cm in length with a resolution of 0.001 mm.

A ruler (up to 30 cm) or Vernier calipers (around 15 cm) are used for larger objects.

front:
**True or False?**

Water should be poured into the measuring cylinder while it is on the digital balance.
back:
**False.**

Water should **not** be added while the cylinder is on the balance, as a spill onto the electric balance could cause an **electric shock**.

front: Why should you **repeat** your measurements and take an **average** in this experiment?
back: Repeating measurements and taking an average reduces the effect of **random errors**, giving a more reliable result.

front: Define **upthrust**.
back: Upthrust is a **force** that pushes **upwards** on an object submerged in a fluid. It acts in the **opposite direction** to the object's weight.

front:
**True or False?**

Upthrust always pushes **downwards** on a submerged object.
back:
**False.**

Upthrust always pushes **upwards** on a submerged object.

front: What two factors determine whether an object **sinks or floats**?
back:
The **upthrust** acting on it and its **density** compared with the fluid.

It floats if the upthrust **equals** its weight, which happens when its density is **less than** the density of the fluid.

front: A wooden block has a density of 0.9 g/cm³ and freshwater has a density of 1.0 g/cm³. Will the block float or sink in the water?
back: The block will **float**, because its density is **less than** the density of the freshwater.

front:
**True or False?**

Density is always measured in kilograms (**kg**).
back:
**False.**

Density is **mass per unit volume**, measured in kg/m³ or g/cm³.

front: What does the size of the **upthrust** on a submerged object depend on?
back:
The **density of the fluid** and the **volume of fluid displaced** (which equals the volume of the object).

A denser fluid produces a **greater** upthrust.

front: Define** force**.
back: A force is a push or a pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object. Forces can cause changes in speed, direction, or shape of bodies.

front:
**True or False?**

Balanced forces produce a **resultant force**.
back:
**False.**

Unbalanced forces produce a resultant force.

front: What is a **resultant force**?
back: A **resultant force** is a single force that represents the combined effect of all forces acting on an object. It determines both the **direction** and the **magnitude** of the overall force experienced by the object.

front: State the two possible outcomes when **forces combine**.
back: Forces can combine to produce either **balanced** or **unbalanced** forces.

front: Define **balanced forces**.
back: Balanced forces occur when the forces acting on an object are **equal** in magnitude and **opposite** in direction, resulting in no net force acting on the object.

front: When do **unbalanced forces** occur?
back: Unbalanced forces occur when the forces acting on an object are **unequal** in magnitude or **not opposite** in direction, resulting in a net force that causes the object to accelerate in the direction of the net force.

front: An object is travelling forward at a constant speed in a straight line. A force is applied perpendicular to the direction of the object's motion. What is the effect of the force on the object's motion?
back: If a force is applied perpendicularly to the direction of an object's motion, the object will change direction.

front: An object is travelling forward at a constant speed in a straight line. What is the effect on the object's motion if a forward acting force is applied?
back: If a forward acting force is applied to an object travelling at a constant speed in a straight line, the object will speed up (accelerate).

front:
**True or False?**

Newton's first law states that objects will continue to move at the **same velocity** even if a resultant force acts on them.
back:
**False.**

Newton's first law states that objects will continue to move at the **same velocity** when there is** no resultant force** acting on them.

front: What is the effect of a **zero resultant force** on an object's motion?
back:
The effect of a **zero resultant force** on the motion of an object is that the object will:

- remain stationary if it is at rest
- continue to move with the same velocity if it is already moving

front: How is **Newton's first law** applied to objects with constant velocity?
back: Newton's first law states that objects with constant velocity experience **no change in their motion** unless a resultant force is applied.

front: Define **constant velocity**.
back: Constant velocity refers to motion at a steady speed and in a **straight line**.

front: In what situation does an object experience **no resultant force**?
back: An object experiences **no resultant force** when the forces acting on it are **balanced**, so the net force is zero.

front: What is the value of the **frictional force** on a car moving at a **constant velocity** with no resultant force acting on it?
back: The value of the frictional force is equal to the **driving force**, as both forces are balanced when the car moves at a constant velocity.

front: State **Newton's first law** of motion.
back: Newton's first law of motion states that: objects will remain at rest, or move with a constant velocity unless acted on by a **resultant force**.

front: When a **non-zero resultant force** is applied to an object, what are the two possible changes in the object's motion?
back:
When a non-zero force acts on an object, the object can:

- change its **speed**
- change its **direction**

front: An object travelling at a constant speed around a circle is **______** moving at a constant velocity, because its **______** is changing.
back: An object travelling at a constant speed around a circle is **not** moving at a constant velocity, because its **direction** is changing.

front: Define **Newton's second law of motion**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Newton's second law** states that the **acceleration** of an object is **proportional** to the **resultant force** acting on it and **inversely proportional** to the object's mass.

front:
**True or False?**

Newton's second law states that acceleration is **directly proportional** to the object's mass. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

Acceleration is **directly proportional** to the **resultant force** and **inversely proportional** to the object's mass.

front: How does **Newton's second law** build on **Newton's first law**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Newton's first law** says an object's motion changes when a **resultant force** acts on it; **Newton's second law** describes that change — the size of the acceleration produced.

front: What is the **equation** for Newton's second law? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
$F = m a$

Where:

- $F$ = resultant force, measured in newtons (N)
- $m$ = mass, measured in kilograms (kg)
- $a$ = acceleration, measured in metres per second squared (m/s²)

front:
**True or False?**

In the equation \$F = m a\$, the force and acceleration act in **opposite directions**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

In the equation $F = m a$, the force and acceleration act in the **same direction**.

front: State the relationship between **mass** and **acceleration** according to Newton's second law. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Acceleration is **inversely proportional** to mass — for the same resultant force, a **larger mass** has a **smaller acceleration**.

front: According to Newton's second law, what is the effect on acceleration of increasing the resultant force on an object? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Increasing the resultant force **increases the acceleration** by the same factor, because they are **directly proportional**.

front: Define **extension**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: **Extension** is the increase in length of a spring when a force is applied, found by subtracting the **original length** from the **final length**.

front: In the spring investigation, what are the independent and dependent variables? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
- Independent variable = **force** applied to the spring
- Dependent variable = **extension** of the spring

front: How is the force on the spring calculated from the hanging masses? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The force equals the **weight** of the masses, calculated using $W = m g$ with $g = 9 . 8 \text{N/kg}$ (multiply each mass in kg by 9.8).

front: The masses are removed and the whole experiment is repeated three times so that an **______** length can be calculated. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The masses are removed and the whole experiment is repeated three times so that an **average** length can be calculated.

front: On a force–extension graph, what does a straight line through the origin show? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: It shows that the **force** is **directly proportional** to the **extension**, so the spring obeys Hooke's law.

front:
**True or False?**

Ruler measurements should be taken at eye level to avoid a parallax error. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**True.**

Reading the ruler at eye level avoids a **parallax error**, which is a type of **systematic error**.

front: Why is a pointer attached to the bottom of the spring? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: A pointer lets the **extension** be read from the ruler more precisely, reducing **random error**.

front: Define **Hooke's Law**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Hooke’s law states that the **extension **of a spring is proportional to the applied **force**.

front: What is the equation for **Hooke's law**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
The equation for Hooke's law is $F = k x$

Where:

- $F$ = force applied, measured in newtons (N)
- $k$ = spring constant, measured in newtons per metre (N m⁻¹)
- $x$ = extension of the spring, measured in metres (m)

front:
**True or False?**

Hooke's Law states that the extension of a spring is **inversely proportional** to the applied force. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

Hooke's Law states that the extension of a spring is** directly proportional** to the applied force.

front: What does Hooke's Law **describe**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: Hooke's Law describes the relationship between the **extension** of a spring and the **applied force**, stating that they are proportional.

front: What is the **spring constant** in Hooke's Law? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The spring constant (k) is the **force per unit extension** and measures how **stiff** the spring is.

front:
**True or False?**

The spring constant (k) has units of **N/kg**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
back:
**False.**

The spring constant (k) has units of **N/m**.

front: What does the **elastic limit** represent in Hooke's Law? **(Extended Tier Only)**
back: The elastic limit represents the point beyond which an object will **no longer return** to its original length when stretched, violating Hooke's Law.

front: What does the green arrow represent on this force-extension graph? **(Extended Tier Only)**\n\n![A force-extension graph showing a straight line from the origin going up at an angle, then curving and flattening out. A green arrow highlights the linear section of the graph.](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/07/56029_force-extension-graph-linear-region){width=1100 height=644}
back: The green arrow shows the **linear **portion of the graph. This is the section that **obeys Hooke's law**, where **force** and **extension **are **directly proportional**.

front: What does the green arrow represent on this force-extension graph? **(Extended Tier Only)**\n\n![A force extension graph showing a straight line that begins at the origin and slopes upward, then curves and flattens out. A green arrow is positioned next to the non-linear portion of the graph](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/07/10713_force-extension-graph-non-linear-region){width=1100 height=644}
back:
